attacks.claim: The public Recent signers panel shows each signer's full name and full postal code. The agreed rule allows only first name, last initial and city, and publishing personal data irreversibly breaches GDPR.
attacks.evidence: • {{ s.full_name }} {{ s.city }} {{ s.postal_code }}

attacks.claim: The newsletter/marketing consent box is pre-ticked. Pre-ticked boxes do not give valid GDPR consent for EU signers, and the consent is bundled with signing and cannot be retroactively fixed once data is collected.
attacks.evidence: <input type="checkbox" id="news" name="newsletter_opt_in" value="1" checked>

attacks.claim: The QA summary reports Pass for the Recent signers panel and for the sign flow, but the template being shipped contradicts the agreed field-limit rule. QA did not test the privacy constraint, so the Pass results do not support release.
attacks.evidence: Recent signers renders 20 most recent confirmed | Pass (template renders s.full_name and s.postal_code)

attacks.claim: The duplicate-signature response is a 409 that reveals whether a given email has already signed a given petition. Anyone can probe emails against petitions, which is an enumeration oracle that exposes political participation.
attacks.evidence: Duplicate signature (same email) rejected with 409 | Pass; ABSENT: uniform response or rate limit on this check

attacks.claim: The sign endpoint has no stated abuse control (rate limit, bot protection, per-IP caps). That allows bulk fake signatures, and the 409 oracle makes automated probing cheap.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: rate limiting or CAPTCHA/bot protection on POST /p/{slug}/sign; load test only covers sustained happy-path signatures at 400/s

attacks.claim: Validation errors are shown only through a red border and background (color-only). sign.js never writes text into the aria-live .form-error element, so screen-reader users get no error message, and the field list is never described. This fails WCAG 1.4.1 and 3.3.1/3.3.3.
attacks.evidence: for (const name of fields) form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid'); ...

attacks.claim: The client handles only 422 and ok responses. A 409 duplicate, a 5xx, or a network rejection produces silent no-op behaviour: no message, no re-enabled state, and an unhandled promise rejection. The submit button is also not disabled during the request, so double-submits are possible.
attacks.evidence: if (res.status === 422) {...} if (res.ok) window.location = ...; no catch and no else branch

attacks.claim: The WCAG 2.1 AA claim rests only on an automated axe scan of the sign page. Automated scans miss many criteria, and there is no keyboard, screen-reader or zoom test. The Recent signers panel, the confirmation flow and the confirmation email are not covered.
attacks.evidence: axe-core automated scan on sign page | 0 violations (no manual or assistive-technology evidence listed)

attacks.claim: The rollback only turns off the sign form. The Recent signers panel is not stated to sit behind the flag, so already-exposed personal data stays public after rollback. The plan also does not say what happens to signatures already collected.
attacks.evidence: Rollback: flip petitions_signing off; sign form is replaced by the existing 'Follow this petition' button. ABSENT: flag coverage of _recent.html and data remediation

attacks.claim: No retention period or deletion path is defined for confirmed signatures, which are kept with email and postal code indefinitely. This breaches GDPR storage limitation and withdrawal/erasure expectations.
attacks.evidence: unconfirmed signatures are not counted and are purged after 7 days. ABSENT: retention for confirmed signers and an erasure request process

attacks.claim: Signer email and postal code are sent to Postmark (a US processor) and organizers receive CSV exports. The document cites a DPA but gives no EU-to-US transfer mechanism (DPF/SCCs) and no statement about where organizer exports land.
attacks.evidence: Confirmation emails go through Postmark; DPA countersigned 2026-09-14. ABSENT: transfer mechanism and export data location

attacks.claim: Organizer updates have no stated unsubscribe or withdrawal mechanism, and the controller/processor roles between CivicSign and each organizer are not defined, even though organizers receive personal data.
attacks.evidence: Optional organizer updates: signers can choose to receive campaign news from the petition organizer. ABSENT: unsubscribe path and controller role

attacks.claim: The rollout gates 10% of petition pages, not 10% of traffic, so a viral petition could receive most of the load during the canary. The load test stops at 400/s and does not model per-visitor 15s polling on a hot page.
attacks.evidence: flag petitions_signing to 10% of petition pages; 400 signatures/s sustained for 10 min

attacks.claim: Confirmation bounce and error thresholds are watched manually for 24 hours with no named alert owner or automated alert. Signatures that are never confirmed are silently lost.
attacks.evidence: Watch sign_submit_error_rate (< 0.5%) and confirmation email bounce rate (< 2%) for 24h

attacks.claim: Email confirmation depends on a single provider (Postmark) with no documented fallback or exit path.
attacks.evidence: Confirmation emails go through Postmark; no secondary provider or exit plan stated

attacks.claim: No stated server-side validation or CSRF protection for the form post; the document relies on client-side checks only.
attacks.evidence: novalidate on the form plus client-side validation in sign.js; ABSENT: server-side validation and CSRF token

attacks.claim: Without JavaScript, the form posts and a 422 response returns JSON instead of a readable page, so no-JS users get no usable error path.
attacks.evidence: fetch-based submit only; no non-JS fallback described

attacks.claim: No attack found: the value proposition is coherent, but it depends on the privacy rule that the template currently breaks.
attacks.evidence: Public 'Recent signers' panel ... so visitors can see momentum without exposing signers

attacks.claim: No attack found: no unbounded spend is evident beyond the polling cost noted under scale.
attacks.evidence: Signature counts update live (polling every 15s, cached at the CDN for 10s)

attacks.claim: No attack found on rendering: the error styling and the consent label display correctly as written, but stale is-invalid classes are never cleared on resubmission.
attacks.evidence: .sign-form input.is-invalid { border: 2px solid #d93025; background: #fdecea; }

attacks.claim: Field names are hard-coded in both the template and sign.js, so a server-side rename silently breaks error highlighting.
attacks.evidence: for (const name of fields) form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid');

attacks.claim: No attack found beyond the items above; the target date and flag plan are internally consistent.
attacks.evidence: Target: Thu 2026-11-05 14:00 UTC · Flag: petitions_signing

attacks.claim: The public Recent signers panel exposes full name and postal code, contradicting the agreed rule that public signer lists show at most first name, last initial and city. Each signer's full name and postal code are visible to anyone who loads a petition page.
attacks.evidence: • {{ s.full_name }} {{ s.city }} {{ s.postal_code }}

attacks.claim: The organizer-updates checkbox is pre-ticked. GDPR requires an affirmative, unambiguous opt-in for marketing-style consent, so EU signers who do not act are enrolled without valid consent.
attacks.evidence: <input type="checkbox" id="news" name="newsletter_opt_in" value="1" checked>

attacks.claim: The duplicate-signature 409 response lets anyone check whether a given email address has signed a given petition. That is an existence oracle for personal data and enables targeted enumeration of signers.
attacks.evidence: Duplicate signature (same email) rejected with 409 | Pass

attacks.claim: No retention period is stated for confirmed signer records (email, postal code, full name, opt-in). Only unconfirmed signatures are purged after 7 days, so the GDPR storage-limitation principle is not addressed for the data that matters most.
attacks.evidence: unconfirmed signatures are not counted and are purged after 7 days.

attacks.claim: Signer emails go to Postmark, a US processor, for EU signers. The artifact cites a DPA but says nothing about the transfer mechanism (SCCs or equivalent) or the transfer impact assessment. The form also does not record a country, so the eu-central-1 routing rests on postal-code inference that is never explained.
attacks.evidence: Confirmation emails go through Postmark; DPA countersigned 2026-09-14, listed in the public subprocessor page.

attacks.claim: Data residency for EU signers depends on inferring the region from postal code, which is unreliable for people living abroad or near borders. Some EU personal data may land in us-east-1, and no fallback or lock-in exit path is described.
attacks.evidence: eu-central-1 for EU-resolved postal codes, us-east-1 otherwise

attacks.claim: Validation errors are shown only by a red border and background, which is colour-only signalling (WCAG 1.4.1). The error text is never populated into the aria-live region, and fields are not linked to messages with aria-describedby or aria-invalid, so screen-reader users get no error message.
attacks.evidence: for (const name of fields) form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid');

attacks.claim: The 'WCAG 2.1 AA' claim rests only on an automated axe-core scan. Automated tools catch only a fraction of WCAG failures, and there is no manual keyboard-only or screen-reader test of the sign form, error flow, or live-updating counts.
attacks.evidence: axe-core automated scan on sign page | 0 violations

attacks.claim: Non-422 failures are silently ignored. A 409 duplicate, a 500, or a network error produces no visible feedback, so the user is left on a form that appears to do nothing and may resubmit.
attacks.evidence: if (res.ok) window.location = res.headers.get('Location');  // no branch for 409, 5xx, or fetch rejection

attacks.claim: Visitors whose signature is a duplicate are not told why, and a network failure produces no message, which adds friction and risks duplicate submissions.
attacks.evidence: Duplicate signature (same email) rejected with 409 | Pass

attacks.claim: The form has no CSRF token, and the 'Follow this petition' fallback and sign endpoint are not described as protected. A cross-site page could submit signatures on a visitor's behalf.
attacks.evidence: <form class="sign-form" action="/p/{{ petition.slug }}/sign" method="post" novalidate>

attacks.claim: The CSV export of signer names and emails is not described as protected against spreadsheet formula injection. Values beginning with =, +, - or @ could execute when an organizer opens the file.
attacks.evidence: Organizers can export signers who opted in to updates as CSV; export is rate-limited and audit-logged.

attacks.claim: The load test covers signature writes only. It does not cover the 15-second polling fan-out for live counts or the recent_signers query per page view, so read-side load on a viral petition is unmeasured.
attacks.evidence: Load: 400 signatures/s sustained for 10 min, p95 210ms | Pass

attacks.claim: Rolling back the flag hides the form but does not address signatures and personal data already collected during the 10% and 100% phases. The rollback plan has no data-disposition step.
attacks.evidence: Rollback: flip petitions_signing off; sign form is replaced by the existing "Follow this petition" button.

attacks.claim: The client assumes fields[0] exists and that Location is a safe redirect target. An empty fields array would throw on focus, and a missing or unvalidated Location would navigate the browser to an unintended URL.
attacks.evidence: form.elements[fields[0]].focus(); ... window.location = res.headers.get('Location');

attacks.claim: The Recent signers panel renders full_name and postal_code publicly, violating the agreed rule that public signer lists show at most first name, last initial and city. It also exposes full postal code, which is more than city.
attacks.evidence: {{ s.city }} {{ s.postal_code }} and {{ s.full_name }} in _recent.html

attacks.claim: Full name is rendered publicly on the petition page, contradicting the agreed first-name + last-initial limit; the release summary claims the panel shows only first name + last initial, so the artifact contradicts its own template.
attacks.evidence: What ships: "showing first name + last initial and city" vs template: "{{ s.full_name }}"

attacks.claim: Publishing full name plus postal code of EU signers without a lawful basis or minimisation breaches GDPR data-minimisation and purpose limitation for EU signers; the agreed constraint is already violated by this template.
attacks.evidence: Recent signers panel exposes "{{ s.full_name }} {{ s.city }} {{ s.postal_code }}"; agreed: "GDPR applies to EU signers"

attacks.claim: The newsletter opt-in checkbox is pre-checked, which is not valid consent under GDPR Art. 7 / ePrivacy for marketing communications; consent must be an affirmative act.
attacks.evidence: <input type="checkbox" id="news" name="newsletter_opt_in" value="1" checked>

attacks.claim: The client-side error path adds is-invalid styling and focuses a field but never announces the error text; the form-error paragraph is left empty and no aria-invalid or aria-describedby is set, so screen-reader users may not learn what failed. The form also uses novalidate and relies on a 422 round trip.
attacks.evidence:
form.elements[fields[0]].focus(); ...

(never populated in sign.js)

attacks.claim: The is-invalid state is conveyed only by colour (border and background), which is a contrast/colour-only signal concern; the axe scan does not verify this.
attacks.evidence: .sign-form input.is-invalid { border: 2px solid #d93025; background: #fdecea; }

attacks.claim: The client reads form.elements[name] for server-supplied field names without guarding against missing elements, and fields[0] may be undefined on an empty array, throwing in the handler and leaving the user with no feedback.
attacks.evidence: for (const name of fields) form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid'); form.elements[fields[0]].focus();

attacks.claim: Client-side redirect uses res.headers.get('Location') on a fetch that may not expose Location cross-origin and also ignores non-422 error statuses (e.g. 409 duplicate, 5xx), so users get silent failure on those cases.
attacks.evidence: if (res.ok) window.location = res.headers.get('Location'); (no handling for 409 or 5xx)

attacks.claim: The rollout watches sign_submit_error_rate and bounce rate, but there is no stated alert on confirmation-email delivery failure or on the 7-day purge job failing, so unconfirmed PII could persist silently.
attacks.evidence: Watch `sign_submit_error_rate` (< 0.5%) and confirmation email bounce rate (< 2%) for 24h.

attacks.claim: Rollback claims the sign form is replaced by 'Follow this petition', but signatures already collected (with stored email and postal code and newsletter opt-ins) have no stated deletion or retention path, and the flag-off does not address data already published or exported.
attacks.evidence: Rollback: flip `petitions_signing` off; sign form is replaced by the existing "Follow this petition" button. No schema changes...

attacks.claim: Recent signers uses confirmed_only=True, but the CDN caches the live count and panel for 10s and the panel exposes personal data publicly; the artifact gives no retention or removal path for names shown publicly.
attacks.evidence: Signature counts update live (polling every 15s, cached at the CDN for 10s).

attacks.claim: The axe-core scan (0 violations) is contradicted by the template's own publication of full names contrary to the agreed rule, and the QA table does not cover WCAG 2.1 AA beyond automated axe on one page, nor the error-state flow.
attacks.evidence: axe-core automated scan on sign page | 0 violations

attacks.claim: The QA report claims 'Recent signers renders 20 most recent confirmed' without evidence that the privacy masking was tested, so the pass result does not reflect the agreed constraint.
attacks.evidence: Recent signers renders 20 most recent confirmed | Pass

attacks.claim: The 400 sig/s load test is stated without the polling load from 15s polling across many petitions and the Recent signers query per page view, so the scale claim is incomplete.
attacks.evidence: Load: 400 signatures/s sustained for 10 min, p95 210ms | Pass

attacks.claim: Confirmation emails depend on a single vendor (Postmark) with no stated exit or alternative path, and EU email data flows to a US provider without transfer mechanism mentioned beyond the DPA.
attacks.evidence: Confirmation emails go through Postmark; DPA countersigned 2026-09-14

attacks.claim: The rollout percentage is applied to petition pages, not signers, and the 10% of petitions split does not limit exposure of PII to a fixed population, and the 24h watch window ends before Friday's 100% step is actually validated for purge and email outcomes.
attacks.evidence: Thu 14:00 UTC: flag `petitions_signing` to 10% of petition pages.
